2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable (comparative institutional and legal-historical case study synthesizing secondary literature and statutory trajectories without a longitudinal cohort or participant sample subject to follow-up loss).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern / Weak control: Historical, macroeconomic, donor, and political confounders (e.g., Nicaragua's 1979 Sandinista Revolution and 1990s neoliberal shift, Costa Rica's 1982 structural adjustment and baseline social spending, USAID/multilateral investment waves, and rural poverty) are discussed narratively, but there is no empirical design or structured comparative control to isolate the effects of legal reforms; the authors explicitly acknowledge difficulty disentangling what shaped CBWM features over time (PDF pp. 8-12).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Key national water statutes, municipal decentralization laws, regulatory agencies, and CBWM legal recognition rules are coherently traced across Nicaragua (1979 INAA decree, Law 40 of 1988, 2003 Citizen Participation Law, Law 620 of 2007, Law 722 of 2010), Honduras (1990 Law of Municipalities, 2003 General Framework Law for Water and Sanitation), and Costa Rica (Law 218 of 1939, 1997 CAARS and 2000 ASADAS frameworks, proposed 2009 Bill Law 17324), but legal descriptions rely on secondary literature rather than primary statutory texts or official gazettes and omit some decree numbers and systematic doctrinal coding (PDF pp. 8-12, 16-20).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern / Weak control: No primary empirical measurement protocol is used; CBWM counts, registration proportions, and access figures are drawn from heterogeneous secondary academic, NGO, donor, and newspaper sources across varying years, and Note 7 explicitly notes discrepancies in national CBWM estimates due to inconsistent state documentation and unregistered providers (PDF pp. 6, 9, 11-12, 16).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Governance and water provision outcomes—including formal CBWM registration rates, post-construction system maintenance, financial viability, water access inequities, and climate-change vulnerability—are discussed conceptually or illustrated with scattered, non-harmonized secondary statistics from disparate years rather than measured with standardized cross-national indicators (PDF pp. 5-13).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern / Can't tell: No study protocol, systematic literature search, or structured comparative coding matrix is reported, leaving potential for selective citation of secondary evidence to support the authors' normative policy proposals on state-network collaboration and accountability (PDF pp. 4, 12-15).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern / Weak control: Country case selection (Nicaragua, Honduras, Costa Rica) is purposive and explicitly relies in part on the authors' prior regional research and expertise—omitting other Central American Dry Corridor countries such as Guatemala and El Salvador—while within-country documentary and subnational examples are selected narratively without inclusion or screening criteria (PDF p. 4).

domain_ratings.justification: Accurately identifies major water governance statutes, institutional decrees, and regulatory bodies across Nicaragua (1979 INAA decree, 1988 Law 40, 2003 Citizen Participation Law, 2004 FISE decree, 2007 Law 620, 2010 Law 722), Honduras (1990 Law of Municipalities, 2003 General Framework Law for Water and Sanitation), and Costa Rica (1939 Law 218, 1997 CAARS and 2000 ASADAS frameworks, proposed 2009 Bill Law 17324). However, statutory descriptions rely entirely on secondary academic/NGO citations rather than primary statutory texts or official gazette sources, and specific legislative/executive decree numbers are omitted for Honduras and the 1997/2000 Costa Rican reforms.

domain_ratings.justification: Clearly conceptualizes the institutional exposure of interest—state engagement in rural drinking water provision through decentralization reforms, formal legal recognition/registration mandates for CBWM organizations, and post-construction technical/financial support—across historical phases from the 1970s to the 2010s, though without standardized quantitative exposure metrics.

domain_ratings.justification: Discusses multiple outcomes—including CBWM legal registration rates, financial/technical sustainability, rural water access equity, and climate resilience—without clear operational definitions or harmonized indicators across the three country cases (e.g., citing a 5-year 30% registration rate for Nicaragua, an unquantified 'minority' for Honduras, and an estimated 40% operating 'outside of the law' from a newspaper report for Costa Rica).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 5-7, 9, 11-13 (Rural water provision at the state-society interface; Case sections; Synthesizing the state role)

domain_ratings.justification: Explicitly states a three-part rationale for selecting the three country cases (shared CBWM rural water model, geographic inclusion in the Central American Dry Corridor, and authors' prior regional research expertise), providing macro-level case selection transparency, although no sampling frame is provided for secondary documents or subnational examples within each country.

Macro-case selection explicitly incorporates convenience/familiarity ('the authors' prior research in the region and related background knowledge and expertise') while omitting other Central American Dry Corridor states (Guatemala, El Salvador), and within-case literature and empirical illustrations are compiled narratively without systematic search or inclusion/exclusion criteria.

No primary data collection or standardized cross-country measurement procedure is reported. Quantitative counts and proportions are assembled from disparate secondary sources (CLOCSAS, Villalobos 2017, FANCA 2006, newspaper articles, NGO reports, and prior monographs), and Note 7 explicitly notes unharmonized discrepancies across sources.

Relies on descriptive historical-comparative narrative synthesis without a counterfactual or quasi-experimental strategy to identify causal effects of legal recognition or decentralization laws on CBWM performance or water access; the authors themselves note the difficulty of disentangling what shaped CBWM technical and normative features over time.

domain_ratings.justification: While the historical narrative notes macro-political and economic context (revolutionary state-building in 1980s Nicaragua, 1982 structural adjustment and higher social spending in Costa Rica, donor-driven infrastructure waves in Honduras and Nicaragua, and rural poverty/population density), confounding influences are not systematically controlled or analytically isolated across cases.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Romano, Nelson-Nuñez, and LaVanchy (2021) present a comparative institutional and legal-historical three-country case study examining the evolution of state legal frameworks, decentralization policies, and regulatory relationships with community-based water management (CBWM) organizations in rural Nicaragua, Honduras, and Costa Rica from the 1970s through 2020. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (as a structured, non-validated qualitative judgment rather than a numeric score), the study demonstrates strong jurisdictional specificity (D2) and rich institutional contextualization (D10) of central agencies, municipal decentralization, donor/NGO coproduction, grassroots federation networks (REDCAPS, AHJASA, CLOCSAS), and practical barriers to formal CBWM registration. Legal source accuracy (D1), institutional exposure conceptualization (D3), and macro-level country selection rationale (D5) are adequate, though statutory descriptions rely on secondary literature rather than primary legal texts. Methodological rigor is weak with respect to empirical selection procedures (D6), outcome operationalization (D4), measurement transparency across heterogeneous and inconsistent secondary statistics (D7), causal identification (D8), control of historical/political confounders (D9), replication and coding transparency in the absence of a formal Methods section (D11, D12), and researcher reflexivity (D13). Accordingly, the paper provides valuable institutional-historical synthesis and policy hypothesis generation, but weak internal validity for causal claims linking specific statutory reforms to rural water service outcomes.
raw_response.overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Moderate-to-weak empirical rigor (strong jurisdictional specificity and institutional context; adequate legal source accuracy, exposure definition, and country-case rationale; weak selection process, outcome/measurement transparency, causal identification, confounding control, coding/replication transparency, and reflexivity)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Comparative institutional and legal-historical three-country case study synthesizing secondary literature and statutory/policy trajectories across Nicaragua, Honduras, and Costa Rica (no primary field data collection or systematic review protocol)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Case selection rationale and research framing in Introduction (PDF pp. 2-4); regional background and Figure 1 secondary CBWM data in 'Rural water provision at the state-society interface in Latin America' (PDF pp. 4-8); country-specific legal and institutional histories in 'The evolving role of the state in rural water provision' covering Nicaragua (PDF pp. 8-9), Honduras (PDF pp. 9-11), and Costa Rica (PDF pp. 11-12); cross-case thematic comparison in 'Synthesizing the state role in rural water provision across cases' (PDF pp. 12-13); normative policy proposals in 'Reenvisioning the role of the state in rural water provision' (PDF pp. 14-15); methodological/data caveats in Endnotes 1-9 (PDF pp. 15-16).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The article has no randomized or quasi-experimental intervention comparator (ruling out RoB 2 and ROBINS-I), no cross-sectional or cohort quantitative dataset (ruling out JBI checklists), no primary qualitative fieldwork/interview/ethnographic data collection reported in this paper (ruling out CASP and MMAT), and no systematic literature search or screening protocol (ruling out AMSTAR 2). Because it is explicitly structured as a comparative three-country institutional and legal-historical case study tracing statutory water reforms, decentralization laws, and CBWM governance interfaces across Nicaragua, Honduras, and Costa Rica (PDF pp. 4, 8-13), it directly matches the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework in RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2.
